Large Loads Tariff Amendment  
Response to Order to Show Cause 
 
Dear Secretary Reese: 
 
The California Independent System Operator Corporation (CAISO) 
submits this filing to (1) enhance its large load interconnection procedures 
through a tariff amendment, and (2) address the issues the Commission raises in 
its Order to Show Cause (Order).1 Taken together, the CAISO and Participating 
Transmission Owner (PTO) tariff revisions supply the tariff-level clarity, customer 
protections, and operational tools the Order seeks. The result is a 
comprehensive near-term response to the Order that can accelerate viable large 
load projects without compromising reliability, affordability, or open access. 
 
I.  
Executive Summary 
 
 
California and the West have an established framework for integrating 
new load growth, including for data centers and other large loads. Through 
coordinated resource planning, long-term procurement of clean and reliable 
generation, and an unprecedented expansion of the transmission system, the 
CAISO and its PTOs are working to ensure that new demand can be served 
without compromising reliability or affordability. This work entails close, careful 
coordination with California’s principal energy agencies, the California Public 
Utilities Commission (CPUC) and the California Energy Commission (CEC), and 
local regulators across the West. It also recognizes that generation and

transmission are complementary investments: securing adequate generating 
resources is only valuable if those resources can be delivered where and when 
they are needed. By planning both in tandem over longer time horizons, 
California’s framework supports continued investment in innovation, 
electrification, and advanced computing infrastructure while maintaining a 
reliable, resilient, and increasingly carbon-free electric grid for all customers. 
 
The CAISO and PTOs have complementary and clearly defined 
responsibilities within this framework. The PTOs lead customer interconnection 
and the development, engineering, construction, and maintenance of the 
transmission facilities needed to reliably serve new and expanding customers. 
For more than a century, that work has enabled California’s growth, supporting 
everything from Silicon Valley and the State’s agricultural and industrial base to 
its ports, cities, and emerging centers of technological innovation. The CAISO 
builds on that foundation through independent, systemwide transmission 
planning, coordination of interconnection and grid-development activities, and 
reliability oversight, evaluating individual projects and load additions in the 
context of the broader needs of California and the Western interconnected 
system. 
 
The Commission’s Order asks whether the CAISO tariff remains just and 
reasonable as unprecedented large load growth tests utility tariffs nationwide. 
The CAISO’s proposed reforms answer the Commission’s concerns through a 
framework tailored to the CAISO’s distinctive market design and the existing 
division of responsibility between the CAISO and its PTOs. The CAISO’s 
proposals constitute a major step toward enabling the timely development and 
interconnection of data centers and other new large loads. The concepts 
proposed rest on a foundation of highly integrated planning and coordination 
among the CAISO, PTOs, State energy agencies, and local regulatory 
authorities, and provide a framework upon which the PTOs will layer their own 
processes to serve new large loads while upholding and reinforcing the CAISO’s 
commitment to reliability. The proposed reforms strengthen accountability and 
protect existing customers. They improve transparency, operational visibility, 
technical standards, cost responsibility, and protection against speculative 
development. 
 
First, the CAISO and PTO tariff revisions create streamlined paths for 
large loads to interconnect to the transmission system while preserving the 
PTOs’ lead role in connecting and serving load. Standardized application 
information, deposits, milestones, study coordination, and service agreements 
will make the process more transparent and predictable. A large load threshold 
and enhanced data requirements will give the CAISO and PTOs earlier visibility 
into a project’s size, timing, operating profile, and potential system effects. 
Coordinated studies, technical standards, telemetry, modeling, ride-through, 
ramping, power-quality, and other operating requirements will allow the CAISO to

The Honorable Debbie-Anne A. Reese 
November 16, 2026 
Page 3 
 
 
identify and mitigate reliability impacts before service begins and to operate the 
grid reliably after the load comes online. 
 
Second, the PTOs will implement just and reasonable deposit, security, 
reimbursement, and cost-recovery provisions in their own tariffs. Milestone and 
readiness requirements will reduce the risk that speculative projects drive 
premature investment, and expanded reporting will provide greater transparency 
into large load requests, study status, projected demand, required upgrades, and 
cost responsibility. Together, these measures align costs with beneficiaries and 
cost causers and reduce the risk that abandoned, delayed, or underutilized 
projects leave other transmission customers paying for facilities built principally to 
serve a new large load. 
 
Third, the CAISO’s tariff revisions close any gaps presented by co-located 
and behind-the-meter arrangements. The CAISO clarifies their treatment and 
requires generator interconnection customers to disclose plans to serve co-
located load, enabling the CAISO to coordinate its generator studies with the 
PTOs’ load-interconnection review. The framework distinguishes service to load 
from generator interconnection service, preserves applicable transmission 
charges and reliability obligations, and allocates upgrade costs based on the 
facilities and service actually required. These provisions give load and generation 
developers significant flexibility regardless of their planned configuration. The 
CAISO also has clarified how developers can submit new interconnection 
requests or modify existing load or generation sites. 
 
Fourth, the CAISO proposes new service options for flexible large loads 
that can reduce consumption when transmission capability is unavailable. The 
CAISO’s Flexible Interim Load Interconnection (FILI) can permit earlier 
energization while network upgrades are pending, enabling the PTOs to provide 
bespoke solutions to large loads based on their configurations and constraints. 
Eligibility, study, metering, communications, dispatch, and compliance 
requirements ensure that flexibility is real and operationally dependable rather 
than assumed. FILI provides a near-term, prioritized solution for large load 
developers, with additional work planned on permanent flexibility and other 
emerging configurations. 
 
Collectively, these tariff revisions will ensure the CAISO tariff remains just 
and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential in the face of the 
challenges the Commission identified in the Order associated with providing the 
transmission service needed to serve the ongoing influx of large loads while 
maintaining reliability and affordability.

The Honorable Debbie-Anne A. Reese 
November 16, 2026 
Page 4 
 
 
II. 
Background  
 
A.  
Large Loads 
 
The CAISO’s work on large loads has unfolded against a rapidly evolving 
policy landscape. The CAISO’s initial focus was to address the most immediate 
operational challenges that could impact reliability. As the stakeholder initiative 
progressed, the priorities and expectations of federal and State regulators for 
large load interconnections continued to develop. Through it all, the CAISO has 
sought to remain responsive to that evolving direction. The CAISO adjusted the 
scope and sequencing of its stakeholder process accordingly, while continuing to 
provide stakeholders a meaningful opportunity to shape the proposals presented 
in this filing.  
 
 
In 2025, the CAISO began regular engagement with the PTOs and formed 
a Large Load Technical Requirements Working Group (LLTRWG) to explore 
possible technical standards to ensure reliable operations as new large loads 
interconnect to the CAISO system. The CAISO’s Issue Paper, posted in January 
2026, described current roles, considerations, and processes for large loads, 
including transmission and resource planning, transmission service offerings, 
cost allocation and responsibility, technical requirements and standards, 
operational requirements, and related issues.2 The CAISO has continued to 
monitor and engage in State and federal regulatory discussions regarding large 
loads and explored central issues and procedural steps that require additional 
transparency or new products. On June 15, 2026, the CAISO issued a Large 
Loads Technical Requirements Straw Proposal on behalf of the LLTRWG in 
order to stay ahead of any potential operational concerns that large loads may 
present. As NERC’s work on large loads ramped up, the LLTRWG focused on 
responding to NERC alerts and inquiries to help share eventual reliability 
standards. 
 
On June 18, 2026, the CAISO and PTOs received the Order to Show 
Cause with the other ISO/RTOs.3 The CAISO immediately re-scoped its large 
load stakeholder initiative to work with stakeholders to address each issue in the 
Order. The CAISO’s work included weekly coordination meetings with all of its 
PTOs, and continuous discussions with local regulators and stakeholders. 
Several major large load developers participated actively in the CAISO’s 
stakeholder process, including Google, Microsoft, Tesla, and the California Large 
Energy Consumers Association. The CAISO received written comments on its 
proposal to address the Order from the following parties: American Clean Power-

Independent of this proceeding, the CAISO’s work with stakeholders and 
regulators continues, and with cause for optimism. As described in the CAISO’s 
30-day informational report on resource sufficiency to serve large loads,7 current 
State planning forecasts and procurement trajectories indicate that California can 
accommodate the large load growth reflected in the adopted demand forecast, 
provided planned resource additions, procurement and transmission 
development continue to materialize. As of January 2026, the CEC forecasts that 
data center load in the CAISO-managed grid will increase by 1.8 GW by 2030 
and 4.7 GW by 2035.8 The CAISO also is aware that utilities are receiving an 
increasing number of large load interconnection and service applications, and is 
committed to staying ahead of the curve, with the timely serving of new energy 
demand reliably and affordably. To date, California’s integrated resource 
planning efforts have resulted in more than 37 GW of nameplate new generation

coordination between the CAISO, State agencies, and local regulatory authorities 
on demand forecasts and resource planning provides a pathway for proactive 
transmission planning that anticipates emerging large load growth by aligning 
that growth with commensurate resource and infrastructure development to serve 
new loads. This will enable the CAISO to accommodate growth reliably and 
affordably.  
 
 
The CAISO and PTOs coordinated closely throughout the development of 
their respective proposals. Consistent with their distinct tariff responsibilities and 
governance processes, each entity developed and submitted its own tariff 
revisions. The CAISO’s proposals are designed to complement the PTOs’ filings 
while preserving the existing allocation of responsibilities. 
 
B. 
Key CAISO Differences  
 
1. 
Capacity Requirements 
 
The CAISO’s approach to large loads differs from approaches advanced 
in other ISO/RTO regions because the CAISO does not condition large load 
interconnection on a requirement to “bring your own generation.” Rather than 
requiring each new large load to develop or procure a matching increment of 
dedicated generation, California addresses supply adequacy through coordinated 
long term demand forecasting, integrated resource planning, resource 
procurement, and transmission planning. These processes are designed to 
anticipate new demand and develop the resources and delivery infrastructure 
needed to serve it. Continued generation and storage additions are expected to 
support forecast load growth, subject to timely procurement and project 
development. As such, the CAISO currently can accommodate large loads 
without making each customer’s energization and transmission service 
contingent on completion of a separate generation project. At the same time, the 
CAISO recognizes that resource sufficiency depends on the realization of 
planned additions, and large loads may develop faster than forecast or 
procurement processes anticipate. For this reason, the CAISO continually works 
with the California energy agencies on forecasting, procurement, and planning.10  
The CAISO will continue assessing whether new loads create incremental 
reliability risks; however, at this time, a bring-your-own generation requirement is 
not a condition for interconnection or transmission service.

This distinction can remove an important barrier to timely service: a large 
load customer need not independently secure new generating capacity or satisfy 
a separate CAISO forward-capacity-market requirement as a condition of 
interconnection. The CAISO has no centralized forward capacity market; instead, 
serving load remains subject to the resource adequacy obligations applicable to 
its load-serving entity (LSE) and the requirements of the relevant local regulatory 
authority. The absence of a customer-specific generation requirement therefore 
does not eliminate advance capacity procurement obligations or guarantee 
immediate service at every location. Large loads must still complete applicable 
interconnection studies, satisfy technical and operating requirements, and fund or 
await required facilities and network upgrades. The resulting framework 
facilitates access to the shared grid without requiring a one-for-one pairing of 
each new load with new generation, while preserving the planning, procurement, 
and cost-responsibility safeguards necessary to protect reliability and existing 
customers. This framework has enabled the construction of many data centers, 
including those supporting Silicon Valley, for several years. 
 
This distinction also explains why the CAISO does not propose to replicate 
generation-linked mechanisms developed or proposed in other ISO/RTO regions. 
Where a large load’s access to service depends on identifying sufficient 
incremental generation, special arrangements may be needed to pair the load 
with a generating project, coordinate their development schedules, or condition 
the load’s operation on the availability of designated supply. Those arrangements 
address a constraint that the CAISO’s framework does not impose: a large load 
customer need not sponsor a corresponding generation project to obtain 
interconnection. Adopting mechanisms whose principal purpose is to satisfy or 
provide an exception to that requirement would therefore add complexity without 
removing a comparable barrier to service in the CAISO. The relevant question is 
not whether another region has adopted a particular innovation, but whether the 
condition that makes that innovation necessary exists under the CAISO’s market 
and regulatory framework. 
 
The CAISO’s proposed reforms in the instant filing instead focus on the 
constraints that actually govern a large load’s ability to interconnect and operate 
reliably: available transmission capability, timely completion of necessary 
upgrades, adequate visibility into load characteristics, enforceable operating 
requirements, and appropriate cost responsibility. A flexible interim 
interconnection arrangement, for example, can address a transmission 
bottleneck by allowing earlier energization subject to operating limits while 
upgrades are completed; it need not also function as a bridge until the 
customer’s dedicated generation enters service. This does not eliminate the 
serving LSE’s resource adequacy obligations or the need to plan and procure 
sufficient supply. It means that those obligations remain within the existing 
planning and procurement framework, rather than becoming a separate, 
customer-specific generation-matching condition layered onto the load

interconnection process. As explained in detail in the CAISO’s Informational 
Report on Resource Sufficiency, the CAISO will continue to assess reliability and 
capacity needs presented by large load growth with stakeholders, PTOs, LSEs, 
and State energy agencies. 
 
2. 
Eligible Customers and Order No. 888 
 
Similarly, the CAISO’s framework for providing transmission access differs 
from the traditional Order No. 888 model. First, the CAISO does not use the 
“Eligible Customer” construct in any significant way. The very few references to 
Eligible Customer in the CAISO tariff are merely catch-alls to prescribe that all 
market participants use a scheduling coordinator to interact with the markets.11 
Second, the CAISO does not offer specific transmission services. As the 
Commission stated in the Order to Show Cause: 
 
Unlike other regions, CAISO does not offer traditional Order No. 
888 network and point-to-point transmission services, offers no 
firm, long-term transmission reservations of capacity, and does not 
provide a formal application process for transmission service. 
Instead, CAISO offers a single “daily” transmission service that is 
available to all Eligible Customers on a day-to-day basis. All energy 
that is transmitted under CAISO’s Tariff that is not associated with 
historical rights or certain wheeling transactions is treated as “new 
firm use,” and those accessing the CAISO-controlled transmission 
system cannot reserve transmission capacity beyond the day-
ahead time frame.12  
 
In other words, transmission service is assumed in the sales of energy and 
ancillary services. Stakeholders agreed with the suggestions in the Commission’s 
Order that large loads do not warrant reforming how the CAISO complies with 
Order No. 888, which has remained unchanged for 30 years. As such, the 
CAISO’s compliance focuses on achieving the Order’s goals without redesigning 
transmission service or creating a centralized capacity market for the first time in 
the CAISO. The CAISO’s reforms thus provide interconnection services to enable 
large loads to interconnect to the transmission system expeditiously, and without 
jeopardizing reliability or just and reasonable rates.

3. 
Allocation of Responsibilities 
 
The Commission’s Order does not require the CAISO and its PTOs to 
reallocate their existing responsibilities for interconnecting and serving load.13 
The Commission expressly stated it recognizes that the PTOs are responsible for 
conducting load interconnection studies, the Commission “appreciate[s] that this 
role may stem from how CAISO and the Participating Transmission Owners 
allocated rights and responsibilities in the governing documents establishing 
CAISO,” and that the Commission “do[es] not seek to alter that allocation of 
rights and responsibilities.”14 Rather than requiring a reallocation of responsibility 
between the CAISO and PTO tariffs, the Order identifies a need for greater clarity 
and consistency in the applicable tariffs, including a clear identification of the 
entity responsible for studying service to large loads. The distinction is important: 
addressing potential gaps in the governing procedures does not require 
transferring the load interconnection study function from the PTOs to the CAISO. 
Stakeholders’ preference was for the existing framework to remain in place, with 
the PTOs administering load interconnection requests and performing the 
associated studies under their tariffs, coordinated with the CAISO’s transmission 
planning, generator interconnection, and system reliability responsibilities. The 
necessary reforms can make those complementary roles explicit and improve 
coordination without centralizing all interconnection functions in the CAISO tariff. 
 
Although the PTOs will conduct load interconnection studies under their 
tariffs, the CAISO will play a pivotal role as the balancing authority and planning 
coordinator for the CAISO area in reviewing those studies. Because each PTO 
studies requests on its own system, the CAISO is uniquely positioned to evaluate 
study results in the context of the integrated grid, including the transmission 
facilities of other PTOs, pending generation, and the CAISO’s approved 
transmission plans. In its role, the CAISO will review PTO load interconnection 
studies to confirm that study assumptions, load characteristics, and results are 
consistent with the CAISO’s planning models and long-term plans. Most 
importantly, the CAISO will identify any PTO-proposed solution that could create 
reliability risk, whether because it relies on an operating measure that cannot be 
dependably implemented, it shifts or exacerbates constraints elsewhere on the 
system, or it is inconsistent with the CAISO’s planning and operational needs. 
 
The same distinction applies to cost responsibility. Preserving the existing 
allocation of functions allows the PTOs’ tariffs to continue to set forth the

interconnect and serve large loads. The CAISO, meanwhile, retains independent

operational consequences. The CAISO, PTOs, and stakeholders believe this is 
the prudent approach because many of the PTOs have a direct relationship with 
their retail ratepayers and the regulators of those ultimate rates, including the 
CPUC. Likewise, it is the PTOs that will construct and own the network upgrades 
if required for the large load interconnection. As such, the CAISO does not 
propose to issue a new “top-down” cost allocation solution through its own tariff. 
The CAISO believes that the PTOs may develop their own proposals to address 
any cost shifting concerns raised in the Order, and that the current transmission 
revenue requirement and credit mechanisms in the transmission access charges 
can accommodate those proposals.  
 
The PTOs worked in good faith to establish consistent cost allocation rules 
in their tariffs; however, there is little case law or Commission precedent to guide 
what constitutes just and reasonable rates for large loads specifically. Such 
precedent will likely come from these responses to the Order to Show Cause, 
offering greater regulatory certainty in the future. If the Commission requires 
additional tariff provisions or greater uniformity, the CAISO is prepared to work 
with the PTOs and stakeholders to develop an appropriate response consistent 
with the existing allocation of responsibilities.  
 
4. 
Non-jurisdictional Transmission Owners 
 
The Order was directed to the CAISO and all its PTOs; however, the Order 
stated that if a non-public utility wished to be removed from the proceeding, the 
Commission would rescind the Order against them. In such a case, the 
Commission “expected CAISO to respond to this order regarding the non-public 
utility’s CAISO tariff provisions on file with the Commission.”15 Based on this 
direction, the CAISO’s non-public utilities requested the Commission rescind the 
Order, which the Commission granted.16 Importantly, these PTOs explained that 
their exits from the proceeding were not simply a legal issue, but that these PTOs 
were generally unlikely to receive large load interconnection requests, and as 
such, did not require tariff revisions. Morongo Transmission, for example, 
explained that it is a non-load-serving PTO, and has no end users. The Six Cities 
similarly explained that their facilities and transmission entitlements in the CAISO 
generally represent shares of jointly-owned facilities with other transmission

III. 
Tariff Revisions and Order to Show Cause  
 
Although the CAISO believes the tariff revisions in this filing do not 
substantially affect Order Nos. 888, 1000, 2003, 792, 845, 2023, or 1920 policies, 
the CAISO’s proposed tariff revisions meet both the just and reasonable standard 
and the independent entity standard. The tariff revisions address issues unique 
to the CAISO, and were generally designed to work without significant conflict 
with the CAISO’s tariff provisions modeled on the Commission’s pro forma Open 
Access Transmission Tariff and Large Generator Interconnection Procedures. 
The proposed tariff revisions build upon the CAISO tariff with independent entity 
variations previously accepted by the Commission.  
 
A. 
Transmission Service to Eligible Customers on Behalf of Large 
Loads 
 
1. 
Definition and Applicability 
 
The Commission noted in the Order that the CAISO and PTO tariffs lack a 
definition of large load as a new category of load.17 The Commission directed the 
CAISO and PTOs to create an appropriate definition, including a load size and 
interconnection voltage threshold, based on the characteristics of CAISO’s 
transmission system. The Commission suggested that a potentially reasonable 
definition would be Southwest Power Pool’s (SPP) definition of “a new 
commercial or industrial customer, located at a single site behind one or more 
points of interconnection, and that has a peak load of 50 MW or greater, 
interconnects to the transmission system at a voltage level of greater than 69 kV, 
and is not part of a co-location arrangement.”18 
 
The CAISO proposes to define a Large Load as “An End User located at a 
single site behind one or more points of interconnection to the CAISO Controlled 
Grid, and that has a peak load of 50 MW or greater.”19 The CAISO believes this

The CAISO proposes not to include a description of the types of load (i.e., 
commercial or industrial customer) in its definition of Large Load. Unless there is 
a relevant operational difference between the types of loads, the CAISO believes 
that specifying type is unnecessary. The CAISO also wants to avoid a definition 
that results in false positives, false negatives, or disputes about what constitutes 
“commercial” or “industrial.”21 In the future, type-based terms may be necessary 
for different reliability rules, especially as NERC finalizes its standards for 
computational loads. But the CAISO has elected not to specify any type at this 
time.  
 
Similar to generator interconnections, the CAISO proposes to continue to 
adhere to FERC and California regulations on what constitutes a “site,” and thus 
does not propose defining “site” in its definition. The CAISO believes the large 
load definition will adequately apply to large loads comprised of distinct loads 
even if they have separate retail meters. Operationally, such loads would still 
have the same impact on the CAISO transmission system. Moreover, the 
prevalence of behind-the-meter and hybrid configurations in the CAISO has led 
the CPUC and local regulators to address multi-meter and multi-unit sites. The 
CAISO also does not believe that the CAISO tariff is the proper vehicle to define 
a site. In the event of a unique configuration, Commission precedent and local 
regulations are more than sufficient in the large load context.22 Further, under its

The CAISO’s proposed FILI framework fulfills the Commission’s central 
objective of making meaningful service options available to large loads whose 
willingness and ability to limit withdrawals permit earlier, reliable access to the 
transmission system, without importing three distinct transmission service 
products into the CAISO’s unique market structure. The Order expressly allows 
the CAISO to explain how changes within its existing framework can provide 
comparable flexibility, rather than requiring it to replicate the service 
classifications contemplated for PJM. FILI translates that flexibility into 
enforceable interconnection terms: a large load may energize before completion 
of required network upgrades, but only within operating limits supported by 
system conditions and subject to specified curtailment triggers, control 
mechanisms, response times, and verification requirements. Agreements 
executed before energization identify those obligations and the facilities 
necessary to conclude interim service, while incorporation into the CAISO’s 
models and operating procedures makes the customer’s flexibility operationally 
usable rather than merely aspirational. Public posting of those agreements also 
provides transparency into the conditions governing access. Although FILI is an 
interim arrangement rather than a substitute for every feature of the three 
contemplated services, it addresses the immediate barrier posed by transmission 
construction timelines while preserving reliability and applicable cost-
responsibility requirements. The relevant distinction is therefore not the number 
or label of service offerings, but whether the framework enables customers to 
obtain earlier service commensurate with their actual, enforceable use of the 
grid—the result FILI is designed to achieve. 
 
 
As described in Section III.F, below, the CAISO plans to develop a 
permanent version of FILI in 2027. This would allow large loads to forgo some 
identified network upgrades altogether if the large loads were curtailable. The 
CAISO recognizes that permanent load flexibility can have significant value even 
in a system with adequate aggregate generating capacity. Although the CAISO 
believes its tariff is just and reasonable without a permanent option at this time, 
the CAISO is committed to exploring the permanent option. The prioritization of 
FILI is consistent with stakeholders’ comments, especially from the large load 
development community.  
 
E. 
Interconnection Customers Serving Electrically Proximate 
Large Load and Co-Located Load 
 
The Commission preliminarily found in the Order that the CAISO tariff 
appears to be unjust and unreasonable because it does not contain provisions 
allowing an interconnection customer to seek the generator interconnection 
service(s) that reflects the operational dynamics of serving either: (1) an 
electrically proximate large load; or (2) a co-located load, as defined in the Order, 
that has a high peak load (i.e., large co-located loads that are 50 MW or

large load “sufficiently electrically close to the interconnection customer’s 
requested point of interconnection, such that the impact on the transmission 
system of the combination of the generating facility and the load, with the 
exception of the transmission facilities between the two, will be effectively the 
same as if they were located at the same substation (e.g., large load that is 
located no more than two substations from the generating facility).”128 
 
The CAISO has committed to examining electrically proximate co-location 
in an upcoming stakeholder initiative to determine whether it may have future 
value for the CAISO and developers. Stakeholders, especially data center 
developers, agreed during the CAISO’s stakeholder process in response to the 
Order that electrically proximate co-location is not a near-term priority. The 
CAISO thus believes its tariff is just and reasonable at this time without 
provisions allowing an interconnection customer to “co-locate” or otherwise be 
studied with an electrically proximate large load.  
 
The Commission’s contemplated treatment of electrically proximate 
generation and large load addresses a potential benefit of studying their 
combined transmission-system effects, but the need for a separate service 
pathway must be evaluated against the CAISO’s existing framework. Unlike an 
Eastern framework that conditions a large load’s energization on the 
development of corresponding generation, the CAISO does not require a large 
load customer to bring its own generation or pair its interconnection request with 
a particular generating facility. Supply adequacy remains the responsibility of the 
LSE under applicable resource adequacy and regulatory requirements, while the 
load’s ability to interconnect depends on the applicable studies, available 
transmission capability, necessary facilities, and operating requirements. 
Accordingly, to the extent an electrically proximate pathway is intended to enable 
a customer to satisfy a generation-matching condition or obtain an exception 
from such a condition, it solves a problem the CAISO’s framework does not 
impose. The CAISO’s near-term reforms instead target the barriers its customers 
actually face, including transmission construction timelines, coordinated studies, 
and enforceable operating limits that can permit earlier energization.  
 
That distinction does not mean electrically proximate generation and load 
can never produce transmission benefits. The Order’s premise—that sufficiently 
close generation and load may have combined effects resembling a co-located 
arrangement—presents a legitimate study question. It does not, however, 
establish that electrical proximity alone eliminates the need to evaluate 
intervening facilities, the consequences of a generator outage or a change in 
load, or the obligations necessary to make any assumed offset dependable. Nor

interim service reforms that can be implemented now.
